name: Existential therapy
heroTitle: Make room for the questions that do not have a simple answer.
summary: Existential therapy explores meaning, choice, uncertainty, connection, and the limits of life. Learn how philosophical questions can become practical without turning difficult circumstances into a failure to choose well.
panelTitle: A meaningful life does not require certainty about everything.
panelParagraphs: Some questions cannot be resolved once and for all. The work can help you consider how to live with them and what deserves your attention now.

model.title: The question may be how to live, not only how to remove a symptom.
paragraphs: Existential therapy considers themes such as meaning, freedom, responsibility, isolation, connection, mortality, and uncertainty. These questions can become especially visible during loss, transition, illness, or a decision that changes how a person understands their life. The work brings those concerns into conversation rather than dismissing them as overthinking.

Choice is considered alongside limits. A person may have some room to act while also facing circumstances they did not choose and cannot simply change. Recognizing agency should not turn poverty, discrimination, illness, or another person's behavior into a personal failure of attitude.

Existential therapy is a broad approach rather than one fixed protocol or a required set of philosophical beliefs. The clinician should help connect the discussion with your lived concerns, not use the session to lecture about abstract ideas.

panel.title: Meaning is not something the therapist assigns.
paragraphs: What matters may be found in relationships, contribution, creativity, faith, ordinary responsibility, or something else. The work leaves room for your own account, including uncertainty.

example.title: The goal has been reached. The sense of direction has not.
example.intro: A fictional example about a transition after an important achievement.

items.title: The expected arrival
paragraphs: Sage has finished a long training program and expected to feel settled. Instead, they feel strangely empty and embarrassed by the lack of celebration.

items.title: The uncomfortable question
paragraphs: Much of life had been organized around reaching the milestone. Without the next clear target, Sage wonders what they actually want their days to be about.

items.title: A wider conversation
paragraphs: An existential therapist might explore meaning, expectations, freedom, and constraints without insisting that Sage should feel grateful or immediately select another achievement.

reveal.title: How could this become practical rather than abstract?
paragraphs: The conversation could examine which parts of the training mattered, which expectations came from others, and what kinds of relationships or activities Sage wants to make room for. A next step might be an exploration rather than a final life plan.

The therapist should also attend to mood, sleep, functioning, and other clinical concerns. A question about meaning does not rule out depression or another difficulty that needs assessment; the perspectives can coexist.

toolsTitle: Large themes can be explored through ordinary life.
toolsIntro: These are questions to understand collaboratively, not a checklist of existential problems.

tools.title: Meaning and values
tools.teaser: Consider what makes an activity or relationship matter to you.
paragraphs: Meaning can be discussed through specific experiences rather than a demand to name your purpose. The work may explore when you feel engaged, what you miss, and which commitments still feel chosen.
A period without clear meaning need not be treated as a moral failure.

tools.title: Freedom and responsibility
tools.teaser: Distinguish available choices from limits you did not create.
paragraphs: The clinician may help explore where you can act and what the consequences might be. A choice can remain difficult even when it is yours.
Responsibility should not be confused with blame for conditions outside your control or for another person's harmful actions.

tools.title: Connection and separateness
tools.teaser: Explore belonging without requiring the loss of individuality.
paragraphs: People may want closeness and still experience the fact that nobody can make every decision or fully live another person's experience. The work can consider loneliness, dependence, boundaries, and mutuality.
It should not treat isolation as something a person can always solve by changing an attitude.

tools.title: Uncertainty and finitude
tools.teaser: Consider limits without making fear something to conquer on command.
paragraphs: Mortality, change, and uncertainty can shape priorities and anxiety. Discussing them may clarify how a person wants to use attention and time.
The pace matters, particularly during illness or bereavement. The goal is not to overwhelm someone with philosophical confrontation.

processTitle: Keep the conversation close to the life being lived.

process.title: Begin with the lived concern
paragraphs: Start with a decision, loss, transition, or sense of stuckness rather than a theory of what your life should mean.

process.title: Explore assumptions and tensions
paragraphs: Consider competing values, inherited expectations, possibilities, and constraints in concrete terms.

process.title: Clarify a considered direction
paragraphs: The work may help you articulate a position while accepting that uncertainty or sadness remains.

process.title: Review what changes in daily life
paragraphs: Look at whether the conversation supports participation, relationships, or choices that feel more meaningful and workable.

limitsTitle: Depth does not require abandoning clinical care.

limits.title: Not a substitute for assessment
paragraphs: Questions about meaning can coexist with mental health conditions or medical needs. The clinician should assess relevant concerns rather than frame everything as a philosophical problem.

limits.title: Not the therapist's worldview
paragraphs: Religious, spiritual, secular, and cultural perspectives should be discussed respectfully. The purpose is not conversion to the clinician's beliefs or a predetermined definition of authenticity.

questions.question: Do I need to know philosophy?
paragraphs: No. The work can begin with ordinary experiences and questions in your own language. A helpful discussion should become clearer, not depend on specialized terminology.

questions.question: Is existential anxiety the same as an anxiety disorder?
paragraphs: Not necessarily. Concern about uncertainty, mortality, or meaning is not by itself a diagnosis. Significant distress or impairment still deserves appropriate clinical assessment.

questions.question: Can this help with a practical decision?
paragraphs: It can help clarify values, responsibility, and the meaning of options. Practical facts and specialist advice may still be needed. Therapy should not decide the outcome on your behalf.

questions.question: Does responsibility mean I caused my suffering?
paragraphs: No. The work should distinguish choices from circumstances outside your control. Recognizing some agency does not erase injustice, loss, illness, or the effects of other people's behavior.

questions.question: What if I do not find an answer?
paragraphs: A useful outcome may be a more thoughtful relationship with an unresolved question, rather than certainty. Review whether that is helping you live and choose, not merely continuing an abstract discussion.
